question.problem:
Using the definition of the hyperbolic sine, calculate ${f}^{-1}(x)$ given that $f(x)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x-3).$

${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-1}}$)+$
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Let $y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x-3).$ Note that $f(x)$ is a one-to-one function on its entire domain, and $y\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ for $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y:$

$$
x=\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2y-3),
$$

where $x\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Next, we apply the definition of hyperbolic sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2y-3}-{e}^{-(2y-3)}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{2y-3}-{e}^{-(2y-3)} \\ 2x{e}^{2y-3} & ={e}^{2(2y-3)}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(2y-3)}-2x{e}^{2y-3}-1 & =0 \\ {({e}^{2y-3})}^{2}-2x({e}^{2y-3})-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{2y-3}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY-1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ {e}^{2y-3} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we require real $y,$ we must have ${e}^{2y-3}>0.$ However, $x-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}<0$ for all real $x.$ Therefore, we select the positive solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back, we get

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})+\frac{3}{2}.
$$
